questions.question: Two players choose $S$ or $T$; payoffs are $(0,0)$ at $(S,S)$, $(-1,1)$ at $(S,T)$, $(1,-1)$ at $(T,S)$, $(-3,-3)$ at $(T,T)$. With private payoff perturbations of size $\varepsilon$, each player plays $T$ with probability $q(\varepsilon)=\frac{1+\varepsilon}{3+2\varepsilon}$ in the symmetric purified equilibrium. What is $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}q(\varepsilon)$?

Two players choose $S$ or $T$; payoffs are $(0,0)$ at $(S,S)$, $(-1,1)$ at $(S,T)$, $(1,-1)$ at $(T,S)$, $(-3,-3)$ at $(T,T)$. Now each player $i$'s payoff from $S$ (not $T$) is raised by $\varepsilon\theta_i$, $\theta_i$ private. The opponent plays $T$ with probability $q=0.3$ and $\varepsilon=0.2$. Which types of player $i$ play $T$?

In a $2\times2$ game $G$ with a fully mixed equilibrium, player 1's purified behaviour in $G(\varepsilon)$ converges to some probability of her first action as $\varepsilon\to0$. Whose payoffs in $G$ determine this limit?
options: Player 1's, since her own types choose actions by comparing her own payoffs.
Both players' payoffs equally, averaged over the two players' indifference conditions.
Player 2's, since the limit must leave player 2 indifferent in $G$.
Neither: the limit depends only on the density of the perturbations $\theta_i$.

questions.question: Two players choose $S$ or $T$; payoffs are $(0,0)$ at $(S,S)$, $(-1,1)$ at $(S,T)$, $(1,-1)$ at $(T,S)$, $(-3,-3)$ at $(T,T)$. Player $i$'s payoff from $T$ is raised by $\varepsilon\theta_i$; $\theta_i$ is private, uniform on $[-1,1]$, independent across players. For which $\varepsilon$ is it an equilibrium that every type of player 1 plays $T$ and every type of player 2 plays $S$?

In a perturbed game, player $i$'s private type $\theta_i$ has density $f(\theta)=(1+\theta)/2$ on $[-1,1]$, and she plays $x$ if and only if $\theta_i\ge\tfrac{1}{2}$. With what probability does an opponent expect her to play $x$?

In a purified game $G(\varepsilon)$, player $i$'s payoff from each action is perturbed by $\varepsilon\theta_i^a$. Suppose instead that each realized $\theta_i$ were publicly observed by all players. Why would this break the purification argument?
options: Public perturbations no longer vanish as $\varepsilon\to0$, so the payoffs do not converge to $G$.
The opponent could predict each action from $\theta_i$, so it would no longer look random to her.
Public perturbations make every type indifferent, so all types would have to randomize.
Nothing breaks: purification needs only that perturbations are small and independent.
